about: Demography rules read by engine.py on every step; edit them and the next turn uses the new values. A copy goes into each turn's manifest. Rates are per year (one turn).

births.about: Placeholder until a decision model (birth_rates() in engine.py) chooses when to have children. per_person_per_year_by_age lists [age, births per person per year] points, filled in linearly between them, counting men and women alike: each birth counts half to the mother and half to the father, at their own ages, so the rates cover both (half the people are women) and add up over a lifetime to half the children per woman. Derived from a forager-like fertility of about 5.8 children per woman, with fathers older on average and fathering children over a longer span. Gives about 38 births per 1,000 people a year at the turn-0 age structure.

settled.about: Settled segments (leaders.json: their leader's type is settled) have birth_factor x the births above and infection_factor x the infection hazard below. Settled life, as farming came in, shortened the spacing between births (stored food, weaning foods, no long treks with small children) and crowded people together with their animals and their waste. Rough: the Neolithic demographic transition is often put at about a quarter more births; technology will change both.

deaths.about: Causes of death, each a yearly hazard (deaths per person-year) for each tile and age; they add, a cohort's share dying in the year is 1 - exp(-total), and the deaths are split among the causes in proportion to their hazards. Rates are per person over the year, evaluated at the cohort's mid-year age; children born during the year face half a year at age 0.25. Well fed, the causes together are calibrated to reproduce the Siler forager curve that turn 0's age structure comes from (Gurven & Kaplan 2007: life expectancy at birth about 34), split roughly as their cause-of-death shares. mortality_modifiers() in engine.py scales each cause per tile; that is where future infrastructure will reduce them. Listed in the order of the deaths.npy columns.

starvation.about: Deaths from too little food, including infections that kill people because they are starving. Hazard by the tile's share of food need met in the year (consumed / need): none at 90% or more, about 20% dying a year at half the need (hazard 0.223), about 60% at a quarter (0.916), about 99% with nothing (4.6), filled in linearly. Children under under_age and people of over_age and older have the hazard multiplied by vulnerable_factor.

predation_and_accidents.about: Animal attacks, snakebite, falls, drowning and other accidents while working: the sum over the activities of hazard_per_hour x the year's hours of that activity, so about 0.4% a year for an adult foraging about 8.5 hours a day. Farming and herding is less dangerous an hour than hunting.

cancer.about: Hazard a x exp(b x age): a fifth of the Siler ageing term.

other_age_related.about: Heart disease, organ failure, frailty and other age-related causes besides cancer. Hazard a x exp(b x age): the other four fifths of the Siler ageing term.

infection.about: Infections that kill otherwise healthy, well-fed people. Hazard base x a climate factor x (1 + wetlands_extra x the tile's wetland share). The Siler curve comes mostly from tropical foragers, so the climate factor is 1 up to full_to_latitude degrees north or south, falling linearly to min_factor at min_at_latitude and beyond. base is the Siler constant term (0.013) less predation and accidents for working adults.

child_mortality.about: Deaths of infants and young children, beyond the causes above. Hazard a x exp(-b x age), the Siler infant term, multiplied by 1 + shortfall_factor x the tile's childcare shortfall: 1 - (childcare hours given / hours needed), at least 0. Hours needed per child per day by age are care_need_by_age points, filled in linearly (rough: infants carried or held much of the day, little needed by 10). With the turn-0 hours the tiles give about 1.8 times what is needed.
